title: ASML’s Strong Orders Signal Staying Power for the AI Boom
author: S
text:
Daniel Nenni
Founder
Staff member

ASML’s latest results offer fresh evidence that the artificial intelligence investment boom still has momentum. The Dutch chipmaking equipment supplier reported third-quarter sales of €11.7 billion and net profit of €4.96 billion, while raising its annual sales outlook to €44–45 billion. Customers are expressing interest in ordering machines for 2029 and even 2030, suggesting that semiconductor expansion plans extend well beyond the current spending cycle.

The challenge is increasingly supply. ASML says demand for its advanced equipment could exceed available production through 2028. It is examining how to expand capacity beyond previously announced increases, alongside upgrades that allow existing machines to produce more chips.

Why it matters: ASML provides an early window into the physical infrastructure behind AI. Before companies can deploy additional computing capacity, chipmakers must secure equipment, build factories and increase production. Interest in machines several years ahead therefore suggests confidence that demand for advanced semiconductors will remain substantial.

For investors, that supports the argument that AI spending has room to grow. The implications extend across chip manufacturers, equipment suppliers and businesses building data centres. Continued factory expansion could sustain demand throughout this network, even if individual companies experience uneven results.

However, strong equipment demand does not establish that every AI investment will generate attractive returns. Purchasing machines reflects expectations about future business; it cannot guarantee those expectations will prove correct. Long delivery times may also encourage customers to reserve capacity early, making distant demand harder to interpret.

The broader implication is that the debate may shift from whether spending continues to whether the resulting capacity earns enough money. ASML’s outlook strengthens confidence in the construction phase of the AI boom. The next test is whether businesses and consumers generate sufficient demand for AI services to justify the infrastructure being built over the coming several years.
